findings.claim: Ch 3 sets out a six-step ethical decision-making model from Michigan State University and the structural pairing of consequentialist and deontological ethical frames.
findings.failure_mode: mis-cited chapter
findings.evidence: Deep 86-88: the consequentialist/deontological pairing sits in Ch 2.2 'Ethical Issues' (mediators' ethical decisions), not Ch 3. Key Concept 5 (line 22) cites it correctly as Ch 2.2.
findings.fix: correct: Ch 3 sets out a six-step ethical decision-making model from Michigan State University; Ch 2.2 pairs consequentialist and deontological ethical frames for the ethical decisions mediators and disputants face.

findings.claim: The ADR choice depends on cost, time, control retention, confidentiality, and willingness to relinquish appeal rights.

findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to Ch 2.2 mediation paragraph: mediation 'can help disagreeing parties avoid the time-consuming and expensive procedures involved in court litigation' [V] (Ch 2.2, "Court or Agency-Connected Mediation").

findings.claim: The text observes that forcing often undermines long-term success through reputational damage.
findings.failure_mode: mechanism in source but not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 55 carries only 'often undermines the party's long-term success'. Converted source 964-968 gives the car-dealership example: the customer 'may leave negative reviews and will not refer her friends and family to that dealership and will not return'.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to the Forcing bullet (deep 55) the source's car-dealership illustration: a customer who feels she got an unfair trade-in 'may leave negative reviews and will not refer her friends and family to that dealership and will not return to it' [V] (Ch 2.1).

findings.claim: The text observes that pure deontology is impractical for real disputes — most decisions land somewhere in between.
findings.failure_mode: loosened / extrapolated
findings.evidence: Deep 88: 'In real life, it is very difficult to adopt a 100% deontological viewpoint for dispute resolution.' Source 1161-1165 continues: disputes arise from ambiguity, so 'mediators must apply their best judgment'. Nothing about most decisions landing 'in between'.
findings.fix: correct: The text observes that "in real life, it is very difficult to adopt a 100% deontological viewpoint for dispute resolution"; where a dispute turns on ambiguity, mediators must apply their best judgment.

findings.claim: minor breach (e.g., reasonable delay without "time is of the essence" [V])
findings.failure_mode: [V] quote not copied from deep
findings.evidence: Deep 408 paraphrases unquoted: 'late delivery without "time of the essence"'. The distillation's [V] words match converted source 3915-3916 ('doesn't state that time is of the essence') but were re-extracted, not copied from an audited deep passage.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep 408: a minor breach example is late delivery 'under a contract that does not specify a firm delivery date and that doesn't state that time is of the essence' [V] (Ch 7.3, "Material vs. Minor Breach").

findings.claim: voluntarily intoxicated parties (voidable only when severity impaired understanding and the other side knew)
findings.failure_mode: case fact turned into a necessary condition
findings.evidence: Deep 404: 'severe inebriation impairing understanding can void'. Source 3825-3827 states the rule without a knowledge condition: 'if a party is so inebriated that he or she is unable to understand the nature and consequences of the agreement, then the contract may be voided by the inebriated party.' The other side's knowledge is a fact of the stock-binge case, not part of the rule.
findings.fix: correct: voluntarily intoxicated parties (voidable only when the party was so inebriated they could not understand the nature and consequences of the agreement)

findings.claim: Trading on material nonpublic information violates Rule 10b-5
findings.failure_mode: in source but not in deep
findings.evidence: Deep 832 gives the SEC definition of insider trading but never names Rule 10b-5. Source 6956-6958: 'Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, which prohibits the purchase or sale of securities on the basis of "material nonpublic information"'.
findings.fix: cycle-to-deep: add to deep 832: Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 prohibit 'the purchase or sale of securities on the basis of "material nonpublic information"' [V] (Ch 14.1, "Insider Trading").

findings.claim: The foreseeability test runs through tort and contract law alike.
findings.failure_mode: claim absent from deep and source
findings.evidence: Deep 334-336 places foreseeability in negligence (Ch 6.1, 'Foreseeability'). Neither deep nor source ties foreseeability to contract law; source hits for 'foreseeab' are Ch 2.1 ('foreseeable future'), Ch 6.1 and Ch 6.2 only.
findings.fix: correct: The foreseeability test is central to negligence (Ch 6.1, "Foreseeability").

findings.claim: Diagnosis (in source vocabulary): the parties have skipped the ADR ladder
findings.failure_mode: term attributed to source that the source does not use
findings.evidence: 'ladder' does not occur in the source; the deep's own paraphrase is a 'tiered system' (deep 17).
findings.fix: correct: Diagnosis: the parties have gone straight to litigation without weighing the ADR options (negotiation, mediation, arbitration).

findings.claim: Signal: an employee or contractor is being told they must perform a specific duty even if unwilling. Diagnosis: this would be unconstitutional forced labour. Follow-up: structure relief as money damages or alternative service.
findings.failure_mode: rule over-extended beyond its scope
findings.evidence: Deep 420: the rule is that personal service 'may not be used to compel specific performance' (a court remedy for breach). The source does not say an employer's instruction to an unwilling worker is forced labour, and 'alternative service' as a remedy is not in deep or source.
findings.fix: correct: Signal: a party is seeking a court order compelling someone to perform personal services under a contract. Diagnosis: courts will not compel specific performance of personal service; doing so would be forced labour (Ch 7.3, "Remedies"). Follow-up: seek money damages instead.

findings.claim: Diagnosis: potential Rule 10b-5 violation. Follow-up: pre-arrange via Rule 10b5-1 plan well in advance, with predetermined dates and amounts, to access safe harbour.
findings.failure_mode: Rule 10b-5 not in deep; follow-up drops the good-faith-beforehand condition
findings.evidence: Rule 10b-5: see D009. Source 6991-6993: Rule 10b5-1 applies 'so long as it is arranged in good faith beforehand'; source 6988-6989: 'disclosure alone is not enough'. Deep 838 omits 'in good faith'. Advising an insider already aware of material nonpublic information to set up a plan to reach safe harbour misstates the condition.
findings.fix: correct: Follow-up: do not trade on the information; future trades can use a Rule 10b5-1 plan arranged in good faith beforehand, on predetermined dates and pre-set amounts, for safe harbour (Ch 14.1, "Insider Trading"). Also cycle-to-deep: add 'arranged in good faith beforehand' to deep 838.

findings.claim: the source flags this as an ethical issue ("should not be used as a way to keep wrongdoings 'quiet' or to limit consumers' abilities to obtain rightful retribution")
findings.failure_mode: verbatim quote carries no marker

findings.claim: The Chevron exemplar's cost arithmetic ($25,000 vs $2.5 million) is a strong empirical case for tier-up evaluation.
findings.failure_mode: single [AE] anecdote inflated to strong empirical case
findings.evidence: Deep 71 marks Chevron as [AE], one dispute. The distillation's own line 184 says it 'should be treated as illustrative, not as a statistical average'.
findings.fix: correct: The Chevron exemplar ($25,000 to resolve one dispute vs an estimated $2.5 million in court) illustrates what evaluating ADR first can save (Ch 2.2).

findings.claim: Reputational and referral costs typically exceed near-term gains; the source explicitly flags this anti-pattern.
findings.failure_mode: overclaim
findings.evidence: Deep 55: forcing 'often undermines the party's long-term success'. Source 966-968 illustrates with negative reviews and lost referrals from a car-dealership customer. The source says nothing about costs 'typically exceeding' gains, and does not frame it specifically as continuing relationships.
findings.fix: correct: The source observes that forcing 'often undermines the party's long-term success' [V] (Ch 2.1), illustrating with lost reviews and referrals.

findings.claim: A decision can be legal and unethical (forced-arbitration clauses to silence consumers; misleading-but-true advertising). The text is explicit on both.
findings.failure_mode: misleading advertising presented as legal; source treats it as prohibited
findings.evidence: Deep 714: the FTC Act prohibits 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices'; deceptive practices are where 'the seller misrepresents or misleads the consumer'. Deep 724: misleading price information (hidden plan price) is an unfair trade practice. Source 6178: unfair trade practice describes 'deceptive, fraudulent, or unethical methods'. The text treats misleading advertising as unlawful, not legal-but-unethical.
findings.fix: correct: A decision can be legal and still ethically flagged: the text accepts forced-arbitration clauses as lawful but says they 'should not be used as a way to keep wrongdoings "quiet"' [V] (Ch 2.3).

findings.claim: Unconstitutional under the Thirteenth Amendment as forced labour. Money damages or alternative service is the appropriate remedy.
findings.failure_mode: specific not in deep or source
findings.evidence: Deep 420: 'forced labor, i.e. slavery, which is in violation of the U.S. Constitution'. No amendment is named; 'Thirteenth' does not occur in the source. 'Alternative service' is not in deep or source.
findings.fix: correct: Compelling personal service would 'constitute forced labor, i.e. slavery, which is in violation of the U.S. Constitution' [V] (Ch 7.3). Money damages are the remedy to pursue.

findings.claim: Inauthentic CSR damages brand more than no CSR

findings.fix: correct: CSR used as a marketing pitch can damage the brand, since 'consumers will quickly pick up on this tactic' [V] (Ch 3.2).

findings.claim: Failing to file Schedule 13D, Form 8-K, or insider trades on time ... Missing them is itself a violation.

findings.claim: the six-step ethical decision-making model is a structured response to that [bounded-rationality] constraint
findings.failure_mode: distillation's synthesis stated as fact about the model
findings.evidence: OB deep 185/688 carry bounded rationality (Ch 6.4). Business-law deep 141-150 presents the Michigan State model with no link to bounded rationality or its design intent.
findings.fix: correct: Decision-making in legally consequential contexts inherits the bounded-rationality limit (OB Ch 6.4); the six-step model's separation of facts from assumptions is one practical check against it.

findings.claim: Coase / transaction-cost economics (not in source) ... OpenStax does not cite Coase but practitioners ... will recognise the connection.
findings.failure_mode: points outside the corpus when the corpus holds the concept
findings.evidence: openstax-economics-3e-deep 181 and 545 relay Coase (1960) [BT]: with clear property rights and low transaction costs, parties can negotiate efficient outcomes (Ch 12.3).
findings.fix: correct: Coase (via OpenStax Economics 3e, Ch 12.3) [BT] | Economics 3e relays Coase's argument that with clear property rights and low transaction costs parties can negotiate efficient outcomes; the Ch 2 ADR options are ways of lowering the cost of reaching one. Business Law does not cite Coase.

findings.claim: International law coverage (Ch 13) is limited to the CISG and FCPA
findings.failure_mode: scope misstated
findings.evidence: Deep 745-806: Ch 13 covers constitutional clauses (Foreign Commerce, Treaty), customs, treaties, international organisations (UN, EU), sovereignty and the FSIA, comity, act of state, common vs civil law, and enforcement (collective action, reciprocity, shaming). The FCPA sits in Ch 5.1 (deep 261), not Ch 13.
findings.fix: correct: International law coverage (Ch 13) is a survey (sources of international law, the UN and EU, sovereignty, comity, act of state, common vs civil law, enforcement); practitioners in cross-border transactions need jurisdiction-specific counsel.
